item.title: Spyware vendors found a way to make targeted ads even worse
item.description: The online advertising industry has found a new way to make itself even more unpopular, with one adtech outfit accused of helping spyware vendors infect people's phones without them even clicking an ad. Researchers at Citizen Lab say they've uncovered the first publicly confirmed case of a zero-click mercenary spyware attack being delivered through targeted online ads, with devices at Al Jazeera among those infected. The technique, dubbed "AdFection," turns advertising networks into a spyware delivery system. Simply opening a website or app can be enough to trigger the attack, with no suspicious links or downloads involved. Israeli adtech firm Discover-Tech is allegedly behind the operation, according to researchers at Citizen Lab, which says the company acts as a middleman between the online advertising industry and multiple spyware and hacking vendors. "We present technical evidence that the Israel-based company Discover-Tech, while purporting to be a legitimate advertising company, appears to be a front for large-scale ad espionage abuse," the researchers wrote. “In fact, it appears that serving as this bridge is Discover-Tech’s primary purpose." Discover-Tech’s Controlium platform exploits the real-time bidding system that decides which ads appear on websites and apps. Every time someone loads a page, advertisers compete for available ad space and, in the process, receive information about the user's device and location. Discover-Tech allegedly used that data to identify specific targets and serve them malicious ads. One spyware vendor linked to the operation is Candiru, the Israeli developer now known as Integrity Labs. Citizen Lab traced attacks against at least 45 devices at Al Jazeera in 2024 and 2025 to Candiru spyware delivered through ads from Discover-Tech. Discover-Tech didn't have to sneak into the advertising system, as Google and IAB Europe had listed the company as an approved vendor since 2020, apparently unaware of what it was Citizen Lab claims it was doing with that access. Citizen Lab sifted through nearly four billion ad-bidding records and found Discover-Tech ads on more than 70,000 mobile apps and 120,000 websites between March and June 2026. Some reached networks belonging to government agencies, defense organizations, and NATO. Researchers found no evidence that those organizations were infected, but they say the ads could have been used to profile devices on those networks. The researchers said the operation also covertly directed millions of devices toward servers associated with Candiru, although those connections don't necessarily indicate spyware infections. Google has since terminated Discover-Tech's access to its advertising exchanges and removed it from its approved vendor lists. IAB Europe followed suit, while Beeswax, Vungle and Eskimi also took action. Discover-Tech and Candiru did not respond to Citizen Lab's requests for comment, nor ours. item.content:encoded: The online advertising industry has found a new way to make itself even more unpopular, with one adtech outfit accused of helping spyware vendors infect people's phones without them even clicking an ad. Researchers at Citizen Lab say they've uncovered the first publicly confirmed case of a zero-click mercenary spyware attack being delivered through targeted online ads, with devices at Al Jazeera among those infected. The technique, dubbed "AdFection," turns advertising networks into a spyware delivery system. Simply opening a website or app can be enough to trigger the attack, with no suspicious links or downloads involved. Israeli adtech firm Discover-Tech is allegedly behind the operation, according to researchers at Citizen Lab, which says the company acts as a middleman between the online advertising industry and multiple spyware and hacking vendors. "We present technical evidence that the Israel-based company Discover-Tech, while purporting to be a legitimate advertising company, appears to be a front for large-scale ad espionage abuse," the researchers wrote. “In fact, it appears that serving as this bridge is Discover-Tech’s primary purpose." Discover-Tech’s Controlium platform exploits the real-time bidding system that decides which ads appear on websites and apps. Every time someone loads a page, advertisers compete for available ad space and, in the process, receive information about the user's device and location. Discover-Tech allegedly used that data to identify specific targets and serve them malicious ads. One spyware vendor linked to the operation is Candiru, the Israeli developer now known as Integrity Labs. Citizen Lab traced attacks against at least 45 devices at Al Jazeera in 2024 and 2025 to Candiru spyware delivered through ads from Discover-Tech. Discover-Tech didn't have to sneak into the advertising system, as Google and IAB Europe had listed the company as an approved vendor since 2020, apparently unaware of what it was Citizen Lab claims it was doing with that access. Citizen Lab sifted through nearly four billion ad-bidding records and found Discover-Tech ads on more than 70,000 mobile apps and 120,000 websites between March and June 2026. Some reached networks belonging to government agencies, defense organizations, and NATO. Researchers found no evidence that those organizations were infected, but they say the ads could have been used to profile devices on those networks. The researchers said the operation also covertly directed millions of devices toward servers associated with Candiru, although those connections don't necessarily indicate spyware infections. Google has since terminated Discover-Tech's access to its advertising exchanges and removed it from its approved vendor lists. IAB Europe followed suit, while Beeswax, Vungle and Eskimi also took action. Discover-Tech and Candiru did not respond to Citizen Lab's requests for comment, nor ours. The researchers argue that the findings expose serious failings in an advertising industry that allowed a company with links to commercial surveillance operators to operate inside its supposedly vetted ecosystem for years. “Discover-Tech’s mass abuse, privacy invasion, and facilitation for mercenary spyware attacks illustrates structural flaws with the online advertising system, which failed to detect or prevent the abuse documented in this report,” Citizen Lab said. For years, the worst thing about targeted advertising was that it knew far too much about you. Turns out some advertisers were interested in much more than your shopping habits. ®

item.title: Windblown yardangs on Mars | Space photo of the day for Oct. 15, 2026
item.description: null A new image from the Mars Express spacecraft reveals windblown ridges known as yardangs, seen here as wrinkled sections on the left and right sides of the image. (Image credit: ESA/DLR/FU Berlin) A new image from the European Space Agency's Mars Express spacecraft reveals the powerful erosive forces that have shaped and re-shaped the surface of the Red Planet over long periods of geological time. What is it? This new Mars Express image captures Amazonis Mensa, a large, flat mountain on the Red Planet that offers planetary scientists a glimpse into the many factors that can sculpt a world's surface. In this photograph, several features stand out to help illustrate this. Easiest to make out are the large round craters created by ancient impacts on the surface of Mars . However, many of these craters have been at least partially filled by lava flowing across the surface of the Red Planet around three billion years ago, according a statement from the European Space Agency (ESA) accompanying the image. More interestingly, rippled structures known as yardangs can be seen to the left and right sides of the image. These ridges "form as loose sand particles are whipped up by wind and deployed a little like a cosmic sandblaster," according to ESA. In the image, the two groups of yardangs ripple across the Martian surface in two different directions. This is because Amazonis Mensa acts as a windbreak, pushing material blown by winds in separate orientations. Why is it incredible? For over 20 years, Mars Express has been providing scientists with an unparalleled look at the Martian surface, helping us better understand the forces that have shaped the Red Planet over eons.

item.title: Bank of America had to bring in 1,000 contractors to patch all the bugs Mythos identified
item.description: Bank of America recruited an additional 1,000 contractors to help patch all the vulnerabilities discovered by Anthropic’s Mythos model, the CEO said on Wednesday. Brian Moynihan, chairman and CEO at BoA, said during the company’s Q3 earnings call that it spent “a couple of hundred million plus” in remediation costs related to Mythos, and the anti-money laundering (AML) orders issued this week. These costs are expected to decline over time, though, with the contractors in place to help ease the initial burden of patching a large number of flaws, an issue that shouldn’t be so pronounced in the longer term. He went on to tell CNBC that the bank brought in outside help after concerns grew over how it would quickly tackle all the work associated with Mythos’ discoveries. The same concerns were shared globally, in part due to how Anthropic marketed Mythos as an all-powerful model that threatened the status quo of cybersecurity. While it ultimately turned out to be highly effective and capable of identifying complex vulnerabilities quicker than humans, leading to the massive influx of patches, some early adopters say it was no smarter than elite researchers. Mozilla CTO Bobby Holley said in April: "So far we've found no category or complexity of vulnerability that humans can find that this model can't," after Mythos found 271 flaws in Firefox 150. "We also haven't seen any bugs that couldn't have been found by an elite human researcher." The 1,000 contractors brought in by the bank in its Q2 added to its existing 3,000 technical staff. The contractors remain at the bank for now, although their assistance won’t be needed in the longer term. Moynihan told financial analysts on the bank’s earnings call that BoA has made its tech engineering workforce around 10 percent more efficient, and that each of the circa 130 AI-related projects it has running is expected to achieve a 2x or 3x return on investment over time. In 2026 alone, the CEO expects AI projects to deliver between $250 million and $300 million in benefits – a sum he expects to shoot up to $700 million by the end of 2027. He didn't detail how. The bank has also reduced around 3,000 roles, including a 5 percent decrease in the number of managers on the payroll, although it didn't specify how much of a role AI played. Moynihan didn’t break down how much of the “couple of hundred million plus” in remediation costs were devoted to AI or Mythos, compared to costs associated with cleaning up its AML issues, both of which the CEO lumped together. BoA’s share price slid more than 8 percent on Wednesday morning after it reported a 17 percent drop in profits owing to the $1.21 billion settlement it agreed to with the Treasury’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN). The FinCEN order relates to BoA’s failure to police national security risks, including Chinese money laundering, and a failure to report over $5 billion in suspicious activity. He went on to tell CNBC that the bank brought in outside help after concerns grew over how it would quickly tackle all the work associated with Mythos’ discoveries. The same concerns were shared globally, in part due to how Anthropic marketed Mythos as an all-powerful model that threatened the status quo of cybersecurity. Mozilla CTO Bobby Holley said in April: "So far we've found no category or complexity of vulnerability that humans can find that this model can't," after Mythos found 271 flaws in Firefox 150. "We also haven't seen any bugs that couldn't have been found by an elite human researcher." The 1,000 contractors brought in by the bank in its Q2 added to its existing 3,000 technical staff. The contractors remain at the bank for now, although their assistance won’t be needed in the longer term. Moynihan told financial analysts on the bank’s earnings call that BoA has made its tech engineering workforce around 10 percent more efficient, and that each of the circa 130 AI-related projects it has running is expected to achieve a 2x or 3x return on investment over time. In 2026 alone, the CEO expects AI projects to deliver between $250 million and $300 million in benefits – a sum he expects to shoot up to $700 million by the end of 2027. He didn't detail how. BoA’s share price slid more than 8 percent on Wednesday morning after it reported a 17 percent drop in profits owing to the $1.21 billion settlement it agreed to with the Treasury’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN). The FinCEN order relates to BoA’s failure to police national security risks, including Chinese money laundering, and a failure to report over $5 billion in suspicious activity. FinCEN’s order was issued concurrently with a $750 million penalty from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, related to Bank Secrecy Act and AML compliance deficiencies. BoA also agreed an $11.6 million settlement with the Office of Foreign Assets Control for sanctions violations, including those related to Iran, Russia, narcotics, and global terrorism. ®

item.title: How Do Fungi Keep the Planet Healthy?
item.description: People may think of soil as just dirt, but it is anything but inert. Beneath your feet, a vast network of mycorrhizal fungi is hard at work, trading minerals with plant roots. This trading system helps enrich the soil, and it sequesters 13 billion tons of atmospheric carbon dioxide each year — roughly equivalent to one-third of the world’s fossil-fuel emissions. item.title: TSMC sends scouts to check whether America's datacenters can deliver
item.description: TSMC is dispatching personnel to check out US datacenter construction and power availability as it plans billions of dollars in additional chipmaking capacity. The Taiwanese chipmaking giant warned of pressure on consumer markets during its third-quarter earnings call, while maintaining that AI demand - at least for now - continues to outstrip supply. "Looking ahead, we continue to observe consumer and price-sensitive end market segments are being challenged due to the impact of rising component prices and macroeconomic uncertainties. As such, we are being prudent in our business planning going into 2027," said chairman and CEO C.C. Wei. Wei said AI demand remained strong, with CPUs for agentic workloads and networking chips adding to the need for silicon. "Therefore, semiconductors will remain essential in the AI mega trend. The value of semiconductors in the global supply chain is set to continue to increase in our view," he stated. TSMC expects capital expenditure of $60 billion to $64 billion this year. Spending across 2026-2028 is expected to exceed the total for 2023-2025 as it expands capacity for customers. Those plans depend on more than customers ordering chips: the datacenters housing them also need power, networking, memory, and other infrastructure. TSMC is checking how those pieces are coming together before committing to expanding capacity further. TSMC is planning roughly 20 leading-edge manufacturing and advanced-packaging facilities in Taiwan and overseas over the next several years, and Wei said the contract manufacturer is also focusing on capacity optimization across production nodes to generate more wafer output. One analyst on the earnings call asked whether power shortages, datacenter construction delays, advanced-packaging constraints, or limited supplies of high-bandwidth memory (HBM) could hold back projected growth. Wei said TSMC factors these constraints into its capacity planning. "We put every possibility we can, talking about the cloud service providers, capex, datacenter build-out, financial, power supply, and also other component supply, all into our consideration. "We make our own judgment, and then based on our assessment of the demand, we still think the demand is higher than the supply, and we are working very hard to narrow the gap." However, he declined to directly answer a question about whether he expected tightness in the wafer supply to be greater next year than this year, saying "the demand is extremely robust and getting higher and higher." Wei said preparations for A14, TSMC's next-generation process marketed as 1.4 nm, were underway. He expects it to become a bigger business than the current 2 nm generation. Risk production – an initial manufacturing phase ahead of commercial ramp-up – is scheduled for 2027, followed by volume production in 2028. For the third quarter ended September 30, 2026, TSMC reported revenue of $46.72 billion, an increase of 41.2 percent on the same period a year ago. Looking

Looking to the fourth quarter, the company expects another jump in revenue, to between $52.3 billion and $54.3 billion. At the midpoint, that would represent roughly 58 percent year-on-year growth. ®

item.title: Beat light pollution with these six portable telescopes
item.description: Light pollution is the astronomer's biggest enemy, especially if you're gazing into deep space. And while some of the best telescopes can make a difference, there's no way to eliminate it. That's why, if you want to observe the cosmos without obstruction, you need to seek out darker skies, get a smart telescope or combine the two. You don't have to book a flight to a dark sky reserve ; just traveling away from suburbia can be enough. That's where portable telescopes come in. Set one up in a field, for example, and you'll get a vastly improved view of the cosmos. Galaxies, nebulas and other deep space objects become more detailed when they're not washed out by skyglow. We've picked out six telescopes you can take on the road: Some, such as the DwarfLab Dwarf Mini, are small enough you could even put them in a backpack and hop on your bicycle. All but one are smart telescopes , meaning that when you do get to your desired location, you can pick from a list of stellar sights to home in on. And while they may be portable, they're powerful with it. So, beat light pollution and say hello to stunning views of the night sky. ZWO Seestar S30 Pro ZWO Seestar S50 Pro DwarfLab Dwarf Mini Celestron NexStar 4SE Vaonis Vespera II Celestron Astro Fi 102

item.title: Praise Otito Obanya: What Is Our Society’s Definition of the “Strong Woman”?
item.description: A thoughtful young woman sits in a relaxed pose in a serene bedroom, reflecting peacefully. Photo credit: Alex Green/Pexels . You have probably heard a woman described as strong. But have you ever considered why such an adjective was used for the woman? In my relatively short time on earth, when a woman is described as strong , in some cases, the description was well deserved. However, in many others, the term was used for women who were grossly disadvantaged, mistreated or burdened by unfair expectations, yet continued to endure them. It was used to describe women who diminished themselves to accommodate unfairness. It is this version of the strong woman that this essay examines. She will henceforth be referred to as TSW. In many Nigerian societies, who is TSW? TSW is the woman with a philandering husband who, rather than prioritising her own well-being, is encouraged to tolerate his behaviour at the risk of losing her peace of mind, her health, and sometimes even her life. TSW is the woman who is expected to live as though her skin is made of titanium rather than flesh. She endures the beatings of the loving man in her life, who is merely correcting her because he wants her to become a better version of herself. TSW is applauded by society for remaining in abusive relationships. She is praised as a good woman, an ideal woman, a strong woman. She is encouraged to stay and endure because of her children. Apparently, a toxic environment plays a tremendous role in a child’s healthy development. A woman once told me the story of how her husband’s infidelity resulted in a child six years ago. She had thought she had found a way to live with it, especially as the child did not live with them in their matrimonial home. However, her husband recently decided to bring the child home, and she did not think she could bear that because she would then be confronted daily with a reminder of his betrayal. She was therefore seeking advice on how to handle the situation. The argument could be made that she should have ended the marriage six years earlier when she discovered the infidelity, particularly given how deeply she was affected by the betrayal. By her own account, the incident caused her significant pain, but she chose to bury those emotions. Ultimately, whether she should have left the marriage is a personal matter. The focus here is not on judging her decision, but on examining the expectations society places on women in such situations. Had the roles been reversed and her husband discovered that she had a child with another man, many people would likely have considered ending the marriage understandable, if not justified. Why then are women so often expected to endure similar betrayals as proof of virtue, devotion or strength? item.dc:creator: Praise Otito Obanya
item.content:encoded: A thoughtful young woman sits in a relaxed pose in a serene bedroom, reflecting peacefully. Photo credit: Alex Green/Pexels . You have probably heard a woman described as strong. But have you ever considered why such an adjective was used for the woman? In my relatively short time on earth, when a woman is described as strong , in some cases, the description was well deserved. However, in many others, the term was used for women who were grossly disadvantaged, mistreated or burdened by unfair expectations, yet continued to endure them. It was used to describe women who diminished themselves to accommodate unfairness. It is this version of the strong woman that this essay examines. She will henceforth be referred to as TSW. In many Nigerian societies, who is TSW? TSW is the woman with a philandering husband who, rather than prioritising her own well-being, is encouraged to tolerate his behaviour at the risk of losing her peace of mind, her health, and sometimes even her life. TSW is the woman who is expected to live as though her skin is made of titanium rather than flesh. She endures the beatings of the loving man in her life, who is merely correcting her because he wants her to become a better version of herself. TSW is applauded by society for remaining in abusive relationships. She is praised as a good woman, an ideal woman, a strong woman. She is encouraged to stay and endure because of her children. Apparently, a toxic environment plays a tremendous role in a child’s healthy development. A woman once told me the story of how her husband’s infidelity resulted in a child six years ago. She had thought she had found a way to live with it, especially as the child did not live with them in their matrimonial home. However, her husband recently decided to bring the child home, and she did not think she could bear that because she would then be confronted daily with a reminder of his betrayal. She was therefore seeking advice on how to handle the situation. The argument could be made that she should have ended the marriage six years earlier when she discovered the infidelity, particularly given how deeply she was affected by the betrayal. By her own account, the incident caused her significant pain, but she chose to bury those emotions. Ultimately, whether she should have left the marriage is a personal matter. The focus here is not on judging her decision, but on examining the expectations society places on women in such situations. Had the roles been reversed and her husband discovered that she had a child with another man, many people would likely have considered ending the marriage understandable, if not justified. Why then are women so often expected to endure similar betrayals as proof of virtue, devotion or strength? Therefore, in society’s eyes, as a prime example of TSW, she had to forgive and stay in the marriage, even if she was badly hurt. She had to keep her emotions buried, but emotions can be like a flood breaking through a dam. Six years later, after being society’s shining example of TSW, she found herself having to confront the pain of her husband’s infidelity all over again. I am not sure how the story ended, but as far as society is concerned, she most likely had two options: Continue being the perfect template of TSW and bury her feelings once again to preserve the marriage and please her husband, or lose her TSW credibility by becoming a woman who speaks her mind and recognises that her wellbeing is just as important as the needs of her husband. Meanwhile, there are several variations of TSW: She is the woman who eventually contracts HIV/AIDS or another sexually transmitted disease from the man she stood by because she would not let another woman take him or give up her family for a stranger. There are people who will encourage her to remain strong, but will never question why the man she clung to so tightly did not value their relationship and family as much as she did. Because if he did, he would not have engaged in behaviour that endangered both. Another variation is the woman who ends up in an early grave after years of beatings, leaving behind the very children who were often presented as her reason for remaining with the oppressor. She is the woman who, even when physically ill, is still expected to carry out every domestic chore. She is the woman who, despite not being abused, is celebrated for giving birth only to male children. She stands in sharp contrast to those weak women who have only daughters. Apparently, giving birth to female children involves no labour pains, and women who bear only daughters experience a birthing process akin to those of marsupials and herd animals. More remarkably, TSW is somehow credited with determining the child’s sex, as though biology itself bends to accommodate her strength. Sadly, when the chickens come home to roost, and TSW begins to suffer the physical, emotional, psychological, social, or economic consequences of years of abuse, she becomes a foolish woman in the eyes of the same society that once celebrated her as TSW for enduring atrocities no human being should have to endure. No longer admired, she is now ridiculed, blamed, and used as a cautionary tale. Her children, who were often presented as the reason she should remain in that hell, either lose her entirely or are left with only a shell of the woman she once was. After years of growing up in a toxic environment, they carry deep trauma, fear, and, in some cases, a greater likelihood of perpetuating the same harmful patterns they witnessed. This article, despite its sarcastic tone, is not meant to belittle the challenges that come with being in abusive relationships or to mock those who find themselves in such situations. Rather, it is meant to help women understand that you do not have to be resilient at the expense of your well-being to be strong. You should never allow the popular question, “What will people say?” to stop you from doing what is right for you. It is also intended as a wake-up call for society to examine its definition of TSW. TSW therefore needs to be redefined. The term should never be used to excuse, accommodate, encourage, or tolerate abuse, unfairness or injustice. Instead, it should be used to encourage women to speak up against unfairness, stand firm in their refusal to be relegated to the background or treated as inferior, pursue their dreams, and become sources of inspiration to those around them. Strength should not be measured by how much suffering a woman can endure, but by her willingness to value her dignity, protect her well-being, and stand up for herself when faced with unfairness. So, the next time you hear a woman being referred to as a “strong woman,” ask whether the compliment is truly to her credit, or it is to her detriment. The post Praise Otito Obanya: What Is Our Society’s Definition of the “Strong Woman”? appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today! .

item.title: X purges 13,000 accounts linked to suspected meddling ahead of US midterms
item.description: X says it has nuked more than 13,000 accounts involved in three suspected foreign influence operations targeting US political debate. In a post on Wednesday evening, the platform linked the operations to Iran, Russia, and China. It said the networks used inauthentic accounts to post and amplify political content targeting candidates and public figures across the political spectrum. The announcement comes ahead of the US midterm elections on November 3. "People come to X to talk about what's happening in the world, including the upcoming 2026 US midterms," the platform said. "Free speech is the bedrock of a functioning democracy, and we are proud that X is the global town square where these debates happen. Our job is to keep that conversation authentic, open, and safe." X did not publicly explain the evidence behind its attribution. Separately, it highlighted its Civic Integrity policy, which covers misleading information about how, when, and where to vote, as well as content intended to discourage participation. Reports submitted under "Civic Integrity" are routed into requests for Community Notes. X says it uses the crowdsourced feature alongside platform moderation and may label policy-breaking posts in critical cases. Community Notes has faced scrutiny. When the European Commission launched formal proceedings against X under the Digital Services Act in 2023, it raised questions about the feature's effectiveness for validating a post's accuracy. X's reliance on crowdsourced context follows layoffs and senior departures from its moderation teams after Musk acquired Twitter. Foreign influence campaigns aren't confined to US elections. MI5 chief Sir Ken McCallum said this week that Russia had attempted to interfere in the 2016 Brexit referendum, but cautioned against treating that as evidence it changed the result. ®

item.title: Online ads weaponised to deliver ‘zero-click’ spyware, researchers say
item.description: Discover-Tech’s Controlium software lets clients mass-profile internet users then covertly hack targets, say researchers at University of Toronto An Israeli advertising agency has been serving millions of online adverts that allow “zero-click” spyware to be used against targets, researchers at a Canadian university have said . Citizen Lab, a digital investigations research unit at the University of Toronto, said it believed dozens of devices at the Qatari broadcaster Al Jazeera had been compromised by spyware delivered through ads run by Discover-Tech, which describes itself as a specialised digital advertising agency. Continue reading...

item.title: Rocket Lab pushes back first Neutron launch to 2027
item.description: Rocket Lab has delayed the maiden launch of its Neutron rocket again, due to carbon composite manufacturing issues. It is more than five years since Rocket Lab said it was developing the launcher, a step up from its workhorse Electron, and capable of sending up to 13,000 kg to Low Earth Orbit. At the time, 2024 was mooted as the first launch date. Then perhaps 2025. Then 2026. And now it is "expected to occur in 2027." It won't be early in 2027 either. During a briefing, boss Peter Beck said he expects to complete testing of the problematic components before the end of Q1 2027, at which point it will set a new launch date. According to Beck, Rocket Lab identified problems with a first-stage tank that failed qualification due to third-party processing. The space biz switched to its own internal processes, and things appeared to be going swimmingly until, Beck said, "we identified an issue with the manufacturing process for the propellant dome." The issue was voids that formed within the carbon composite layers during manufacturing. Beck explained, "They don't necessarily mean that the dome would fail in flight," but they would reduce the margin, so a rethink was required. The good news, according to Beck, is that the problem is solved. The bad news? Dealing with it has delayed things. In August, Rocket Lab said it targeted delivery of Neutron to the launch pad in Q4 2026. Beck now reckons the cryo and hydrostatic test campaigns will not wrap up until Q1 2027. Rocket Lab's shares have taken a battering following the announcement, dropping from about $63 yesterday to near $53 in after-hours trading. When it becomes operational, Neutron will feature an entirely reusable first stage with a "Hungry Hippo" clamshell fairing, opening to deploy a second stage before closing for a return to Earth. The timing of Neutron's availability is of note since it could come as SpaceX reportedly seeks to wind down Falcon 9 in favor of Starship. While Falcon 9 can loft heavier payloads, Neutron's mass capability puts it firmly in the same class. Assuming, of course, it makes it to the launchpad. ®

item.title: Scientists discover 'chemical starter kit' for life in planetary birthplaces
item.description: Methanol, coming as part of the 'chemical starter kit' around young stars, has produced some unexpected surprises that could ultimately reveal some of the conditions in which planets and potentially life form around protostars. The methanol discoveries were made by astronomers using ALMA (the Atacama Large millimeter/submillimeter Array) in the Atacama Desert in Chile, as part of a project called COMPASS (the Complex Organic Molecules in Protostars with ALMA Spectral Surveys). "Our work provides insight into the complex chemistry of young star systems and is ultimately an important piece of the puzzle in understanding the origin of life," said University of Bern astrophysicist Maria Drozdovskaya, who leads the COMPASS project, in a statement . Drozdovskaya's multinational team of more than 30 astronomers has been chasing down complex organic molecules, large molecules that include carbon atoms, in the planetary construction yards around eleven young stars. These molecules form part of the chemical inventory that ultimately builds planets and, perhaps, even life that will one day live on those planets. Methanol matters Methanol (CH 3 OH) is important because it is highly abundant in star- and planet-forming regions. In fact, it’s the most abundant complex organic molecule to be found in interstellar space , and is commonly found in planet-forming disks. Its sheer abundance means that, of all the molecules found around young stars, methanol is the easiest in which to detect different forms where regular hydrogen atoms are replaced by a heavier isotope of hydrogen called deuterium. How many molecules contain these heavier isotopes is highly dependent upon the conditions in which planets are forming within the disk. That’s why the COMPASS team used ALMA to search for these forms of methanol in the gas belonging to the planet-forming disks around the 11 nearby low-mass protostars . The observations have also helped assess the general chemical diversity of these disks. The Perseus Molecular Cloud home to the protostar IRAS 4A2 (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) The unexpected discovery of a methanol molecule containing deuterium was made in the planet-forming disk around only one of those 11 stars, namely the young star IRAS 4A2, located about a thousand light-years away in the Perseus Molecular Cloud. IRAS refers to the Infrared Astronomical Satellite, which was a joint NASA–UK–Netherlands mission launched in 1983 and which first detected this young star as a source of infrared light through the thick gas and dust of the molecular cloud. The COMPASS team also discovered methanol maser emission from more than half of the 11 protostars, favoring the youngest of the stars. A maser is a microwave version of a laser in the sense that the microwave emission is being stimulated and then amplified, but astrophysical masers occur naturally, often in shock fronts as methanol molecules collide and are excited. Methanol masers have previously been detected
item.dc:creator: Keith Cooper
item.content:encoded: Methanol, coming as part of the 'chemical starter kit' around young stars, has produced some unexpected surprises that could ultimately reveal some of the conditions in which planets and potentially life form around protostars. The methanol discoveries were made by astronomers using ALMA (the Atacama Large millimeter/submillimeter Array) in the Atacama Desert in Chile, as part of a project called COMPASS (the Complex Organic Molecules in Protostars with ALMA Spectral Surveys). "Our work provides insight into the complex chemistry of young star systems and is ultimately an important piece of the puzzle in understanding the origin of life," said University of Bern astrophysicist Maria Drozdovskaya, who leads the COMPASS project, in a statement . Drozdovskaya's multinational team of more than 30 astronomers has been chasing down complex organic molecules, large molecules that include carbon atoms, in the planetary construction yards around eleven young stars. These molecules form part of the chemical inventory that ultimately builds planets and, perhaps, even life that will one day live on those planets. Methanol matters Methanol (CH 3 OH) is important because it is highly abundant in star- and planet-forming regions. In fact, it’s the most abundant complex organic molecule to be found in interstellar space , and is commonly found in planet-forming disks. Its sheer abundance means that, of all the molecules found around young stars, methanol is the easiest in which to detect different forms where regular hydrogen atoms are replaced by a heavier isotope of hydrogen called deuterium. How many molecules contain these heavier isotopes is highly dependent upon the conditions in which planets are forming within the disk. That’s why the COMPASS team used ALMA to search for these forms of methanol in the gas belonging to the planet-forming disks around the 11 nearby low-mass protostars . The observations have also helped assess the general chemical diversity of these disks. The Perseus Molecular Cloud home to the protostar IRAS 4A2 (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) The unexpected discovery of a methanol molecule containing deuterium was made in the planet-forming disk around only one of those 11 stars, namely the young star IRAS 4A2, located about a thousand light-years away in the Perseus Molecular Cloud. IRAS refers to the Infrared Astronomical Satellite, which was a joint NASA–UK–Netherlands mission launched in 1983 and which first detected this young star as a source of infrared light through the thick gas and dust of the molecular cloud. The COMPASS team also discovered methanol maser emission from more than half of the 11 protostars, favoring the youngest of the stars. A maser is a microwave version of a laser in the sense that the microwave emission is being stimulated and then amplified, but astrophysical masers occur naturally, often in shock fronts as methanol molecules collide and are excited. Methanol masers have previously been detected in planet-forming disks around turbulent high-mass protostars, but COMPASS’ observations are the first detection of them around calmer lower-mass protostars. "The fact that it has now also been found in a low-mass protostar shows that locally extreme physical conditions can prevail there analogously to massive stars and challenges our previous understanding of the formation of sun -like stars," said Drozdovskaya. Some of the antennas in the ALMA array located in the Atacama Desert (Image credit: ESO/C. Malin) The finding implies that methanol masers are a common product of all planet-forming discs and therefore are produced by processes that are universal in star- and planet-birth, regardless of the protostar's mass. For example, thermal bursts from the growing star as it accumulates gas from its surroundings could generate shocks in a planet-forming disk, stimulating maser activity in the abundant methanol. "Both results underscore how important high-performance spectroscopic measurements like those from COMPASS with ALMA are for detecting rare and previously unknown chemical phenomena," said Drozdovskaya, referring to both the methanol masers and the deuterium-rich methanol molecules around IRAS 4A2. "They show just how much we still have to learn about the chemical processes in young protostellar systems." A protoplanetary disk contains the gassy and dusty material that gives rise to planets and their moons. A few planets have coalesced out of the disk in this artist’s impression. (Image credit: University of Copenhagen/Lars Buchhave) The new findings have at least begun to answer some questions, such as how the diversity in this 'chemical starter kit' varies from star to star, with ALMA detecting some subtle differences, such as variations in the abundance of oxygen- and nitrogen-bearing molecular species among the eleven stars. However, questions about how the chemistry of young star systems arises and how it influences the evolution of those systems remain unanswered. For now, the COMPASS team is painstakingly and systematically studying the data on all the different types of molecules detected in their ALMA observations, and preparing follow-up studies with other facilities including the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). "The analysis of all the collected data will take several more years," said Drozdovskaya. The first results from COMPASS are published in seven papers [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ] in the October 2026 issue of the journal Astronomy & Astrophysics.

item.title: Raducanu could secure protected ranking with early season exit
OpenAI claims 100-plus secret files followed ex-employee back to Apple
item.description: Apple's trade secrets spat with OpenAI has taken a new turn, with the ChatGPT maker accusing a former employee of taking more than 100 confidential files about its unreleased hardware back to Cupertino. In a court filing submitted Wednesday, OpenAI claims the unnamed employee, who joined from Apple before returning to the iPhone maker just six months later, transferred sensitive documents to his personal accounts before leaving. The filing alleges the files included detailed images of at least one unreleased OpenAI device, engineering and manufacturing data, supplier information, and project files, along with specifications for cosmetic finishes and reports on coating and sealing hardware components. According to the filing, some were transferred just after midnight in Singapore on June 2, which the filing claims was the employee's final day at OpenAI. But OpenAI claims the information didn't simply disappear into a personal inbox. According to the filing, the former employee also allegedly presented OpenAI's product plans to Apple's senior leadership, including its vice president of operations in Asia. That presentation apparently happened months ago, and OpenAI is now pointing to Apple's latest push into AI-powered hardware, including its newly announced smart home products, as cause for concern. "OpenAI is very concerned that its trade secret and confidential information is now circulating inside Apple, where Apple engineers can shape Apple's upcoming products based on OpenAI's confidential and innovative work," the company told the court. Apple says it hasn't found anything to back up OpenAI's claims and insists it has rules to stop staff from bringing their former employers' secrets into the company. There's a certain irony here, given that Apple was the one accusing OpenAI of stealing its secrets just a few months ago. Back in July, Apple sued OpenAI and former employees Chang Liu and Tang Yew Tan, alleging they took confidential engineering information to help the ChatGPT maker develop its own hardware. Cupertino alleged that the pair took valuable trade secrets concerning its hardware development, including information about unreleased products, to their new employer. OpenAI denied the accusations, saying at the time: "We have no interest in other companies' trade secrets. We remain focused on building innovative technology that empowers people everywhere." Now the ChatGPT maker is claiming confidential hardware information may have traveled in the opposite direction, though it has yet to establish that Apple received or used any of the allegedly taken material. OpenAI has asked the court for time to investigate the matter and potentially bring counterclaims against Apple. No such counterclaims have yet been filed. For all the talk of groundbreaking AI hardware, the biggest competition right now appears to be over who took whose files. ®

item.title: Legal Aid Agency hackers made off with records dating back to 1978
item.description: Hackers who broke into the UK's Legal Aid Agency last year stole records dating back nearly five decades, the government has admitted, revealing the breach was far more extensive than previously thought. The Legal Aid Agency said on Wednesday that around 250,000 records stolen in the April 2025 attack date from before 2007, including one going back to 1978. That's much further back than the agency previously estimated ­­– it initially said the stolen data covered legal aid applications, claims, and payments from 2007. Most of the newly identified records date from the 1990s and 2000s, with only a “fractionally small number” originating before 1990. Still, the discovery raises an awkward question about just how much historical personal information was sitting in government systems when the attackers came knocking. That wasn't the only surprise in the stolen data, as the Ministry of Justice (MoJ) has also discovered that hackers accessed information from HM Prison and Probation Service (HMPPS), including names, dates of birth, nationalities, and case reference numbers for offenders supervised by probation services between 2010 and 2017. The government says the probation records concern a relatively small number of offenders, with more than 99 percent of the affected data relating to people under supervision in 2016 and 2017. It stressed that none of the stolen probation information relates to victims of crime. The latest revelations come almost 18 months after the Legal Aid Agency disclosed that criminals had accessed and downloaded a significant amount of sensitive personal information. The agency first detected the intrusion on April 23, 2025, but officials didn't establish the scale of the compromise until May 16. The government subsequently took the LAA's online services offline, leaving lawyers struggling to access the systems they needed to submit claims and manage cases. The disruption dragged on for months, with the agency's troubled return to service in December leaving legal aid providers battling delays and ongoing technical problems. Further forensic work has now revealed that the data theft goes back much further than officials originally believed. The compromised information varies by individual but could include names, addresses, dates of birth, National Insurance numbers, financial details, and information about legal proceedings. Some records also contain details of criminal charges, pleas, convictions, and sentences. Among the older material are records relating to legal aid benefit assessments dating from 1978 to 2012, and payments made under the Very High Cost Cases scheme between 1981 and 2004. The government cautioned that the presence of historical records doesn’t mean that everyone who applied for legal aid before 2007 had their information stolen, nor does the 250,000 figure represent a confirmed number of affected individuals. That's much further back than the agency previously estimated ­­– it initially said the stolen data covered legal aid applications, claims, and payments from 2007. Most of the newly identified records date from the 1990s and 2000s, with only a “fractionally small number” originating before 1990. Still, the discovery raises an awkward question about just how much historical personal information was sitting in government systems when the attackers came knocking. That wasn't the only surprise in the stolen data, as the Ministry of Justice (MoJ) has also discovered that hackers accessed information from HM Prison and Probation Service (HMPPS), including names, dates of birth, nationalities, and case reference numbers for offenders supervised by probation services between 2010 and 2017. The government says the probation records concern a relatively small number of offenders, with more than 99 percent of the affected data relating to people under supervision in 2016 and 2017. It stressed that none of the stolen probation information relates to victims of crime. The latest revelations come almost 18 months after the Legal Aid Agency disclosed that criminals had accessed and downloaded a significant amount of sensitive personal information. The agency first detected the intrusion on April 23, 2025, but officials didn't establish the scale of the compromise until May 16. The government subsequently took the LAA's online services offline, leaving lawyers struggling to access the systems they needed to submit claims and manage cases. The disruption dragged on for months, with the agency's troubled return to service in December leaving legal aid providers battling delays and ongoing technical problems. Further forensic work has now revealed that the data theft goes back much further than officials originally believed. The compromised information varies by individual but could include names, addresses, dates of birth, National Insurance numbers, financial details, and information about legal proceedings. Some records also contain details of criminal charges, pleas, convictions, and sentences. Among the older material are records relating to legal aid benefit assessments dating from 1978 to 2012, and payments made under the Very High Cost Cases scheme between 1981 and 2004. The government cautioned that the presence of historical records doesn’t mean that everyone who applied for legal aid before 2007 had their information stolen, nor does the 250,000 figure represent a confirmed number of affected individuals. Explaining why it has taken so long to pin down the extent of the theft, the MoJ said the attackers stole information spread across several complex systems, much of it unstructured, fragmented, or incomplete. "Because of our increased capability to identify data, we have developed a more complete understanding of the information compromised," the agency said. The government says it has no indication that the stolen information has been published or shared, although that offers little certainty to anyone whose personal details may now be in criminal hands. Since the attack, the MoJ says it has tightened authentication and access controls, improved security monitoring, addressed vulnerabilities and begun retiring or isolating higher-risk technology. Work to modernize its legacy systems is also underway. The question of why records stretching back to the 1970s remained accessible in the first place is one the latest update does not answer. ®

item.title: FC Copenhagen Women have a ‘startup-like’ brand. Now they need results
item.description: A famous name and record attendances have given FCK a platform but a difficult start in Denmark’s top-flight shows success on the pitch is not guaranteed On an August day in 2024, 5,165 fans gathered at Vanløse Idrætspark to watch FC Copenhagen (FCK) take on B73 Slagelse in their first league match. For Denmark’s most successful men’s club, with 16 league titles, it marked the realisation of their desire to establish a women’s team, through collaboration with the existing FC Damsø, and an ambitious project with aims of having a wide-reaching impact on and off the pitch. The 26 months since have brought a whirlwind of success, the club securing back-to-back promotions to reach the A-Liga. Now they are in the top division and “playing with the big dogs”, as their head of women’s football, Romaney Pinnock, coins it, and they must adapt to stay there. Continue reading...

For Denmark’s most successful men’s club, with 16 league titles, it marked the realisation of their desire to establish a women’s team, through collaboration with the existing FC Damsø, and an ambitious project with aims of having a wide-reaching impact on and off the pitch. The 26 months since have brought a whirlwind of success, the club securing back-to-back promotions to reach the A-Liga. Now they are in the top division and “playing with the big dogs”, as their head of women’s football, Romaney Pinnock, coins it, and they must adapt to stay there. Continue reading...

item.title: US Air Force pilots used malware-laden USB drives to plan Afghanistan missions
item.description: Welcome, once again, to PWNED, the weekly column where we gawk at organizations that have made serious security mistakes. Normally, we’re talking about businesses or maybe the odd school that messes up, but today we’re writing about a serious IT screwup in the world’s most powerful military. Have a story about someone leaving a gaping hole in their network? Share it with us at pwned@sitpub.com. Anonymity is available upon request. Today’s tale comes from Justin Henkel, the CISO of IT monitoring and service company SolarWinds. Henkel previously worked in IT security for the Air Force and one day in the early 2000s saw a practice that just wouldn’t fly today. Before USB drives became popular, burning CDs with mission data was the modus operandi, and those discs were put in both unclassified and classified systems. “They would write a CD, and then they would take that CD and then put it in a classified system and do the remainder of the mission planning,” Henkel told us. “Then they would take that disc and then put it in the airplane.” Inside the airplane, the data on the CD would help the pilot navigate and contain information about threats they might encounter. Later, when thumb drives became a thing, pilots used them instead of discs. “They didn't really think about the overall impact of classified versus unclassified systems,” Henkel said of the pilots. “Using the same device for both, they didn’t understand that you could read and write onto a USB drive with malware. [They were] not really understanding the overall threat picture.” According to Henkel, Air Force personnel would buy their flash drives from local vendors rather than sourcing them from official military contractors. If they were in Afghanistan, those drives could literally come from a store in Kabul. And it wasn’t exactly the equivalent of Best Buy. “It was more difficult to bring a US-based computer into the nation than it was just to buy local,” he said. “So they were just going out into the local market in Kabul or whatever city that they were out [in]. And I used to do this: go out, make relationships with the local vendors. ‘Hey I need 100 USB sticks.’” Unfortunately, enemies of the US noticed and soon started selling infected USB drives to local vendors in the Middle East. Henkel knew that using a sneakernet with classified systems was a recipe for disaster. It’s just that no one would listen to him. “It was just a shock,” he told us. “I was a young 22-year-old guy, very junior in the overall rank system, trying to tell colonels and majors that what they’re doing is a violation.” In 2008, the US Department of Defense was infected by malware after somebody attached an infected USB flash drive to a laptop with access to US Central Command. item.content:encoded: Welcome, once again, to PWNED, the weekly column where we gawk at organizations that have made serious security mistakes. Normally, we’re talking about businesses or maybe the odd school that messes up, but today we’re writing about a serious IT screwup in the world’s most powerful military. Have a story about someone leaving a gaping hole in their network? Share it with us at pwned@sitpub.com. Anonymity is available upon request. Today’s tale comes from Justin Henkel, the CISO of IT monitoring and service company SolarWinds. Henkel previously worked in IT security for the Air Force and one day in the early 2000s saw a practice that just wouldn’t fly today. Before USB drives became popular, burning CDs with mission data was the modus operandi, and those discs were put in both unclassified and classified systems. “They would write a CD, and then they would take that CD and then put it in a classified system and do the remainder of the mission planning,” Henkel told us. “Then they would take that disc and then put it in the airplane.” Inside the airplane, the data on the CD would help the pilot navigate and contain information about threats they might encounter. Later, when thumb drives became a thing, pilots used them instead of discs. “They didn't really think about the overall impact of classified versus unclassified systems,” Henkel said of the pilots. “Using the same device for both, they didn’t understand that you could read and write onto a USB drive with malware. [They were] not really understanding the overall threat picture.” According to Henkel, Air Force personnel would buy their flash drives from local vendors rather than sourcing them from official military contractors. If they were in Afghanistan, those drives could literally come from a store in Kabul. And it wasn’t exactly the equivalent of Best Buy. “It was more difficult to bring a US-based computer into the nation than it was just to buy local,” he said. “So they were just going out into the local market in Kabul or whatever city that they were out [in]. And I used to do this: go out, make relationships with the local vendors. ‘Hey I need 100 USB sticks.’” Unfortunately, enemies of the US noticed and soon started selling infected USB drives to local vendors in the Middle East. Henkel knew that using a sneakernet with classified systems was a recipe for disaster. It’s just that no one would listen to him. “It was just a shock,” he told us. “I was a young 22-year-old guy, very junior in the overall rank system, trying to tell colonels and majors that what they’re doing is a violation.” In 2008, the US Department of Defense was infected by malware after somebody attached an infected USB flash drive to a laptop with access to US Central Command. The worm, dubbed Agent.BTZ, could collect information from infected computers and communicate with remote servers. A 2016 report from the FBI and DHS attributed the malware to one or more Russian groups. It took the Pentagon 14 months to scrub it from its systems. It took this attack for the Pentagon to wise up in 2008 and ban the use of USB drives, instead forcing data transfers to go through more secure systems. Eventually, in 2010, the drives were allowed again under certain circumstances. ®

item.title: Southgate ‘hardly watches’ football and does not envisage Premier League return
item.description: Former England manager last went to game in May 2025 He says he got only brief enjoyment from wins by the end Gareth Southgate has all but ruled out a return to Premier League management and revealed he “didn’t even enjoy the wins” for more than a couple of minutes towards the end of his time in charge of England. Southgate, who has moved away from football since stepping down as the manager of the England men’s team after defeat by Spain in the Euro 2024 final, said he had not attended a game since watching his boyhood club Crystal Palace beat Manchester City in the FA Cup final last year. Continue reading...

item.title: SpaceX wants to launch Starship more than 450 times per year from South Texas
item.description: null SpaceX wants to start flying its Starship megarocket a lot more often. The company has requested permission to launch Starship from its Starbase site in South Texas up to 456 times per year. That's a big jump from the currently allowed cadence of 25. The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) is in the early stages of reviewing the request. Today (Oct. 14), the agency announced "its intent to prepare a Programmatic Environmental Impact Statement, open a public scoping period and hold public scoping meetings for SpaceX’s proposal." Starship, which stands more than 400 feet (122 meters) tall, is the biggest and most powerful rocket ever built. It's also designed to be fully and rapidly reusable, a breakthrough that SpaceX believes will revolutionize spaceflight. The megarocket has flown 14 times to date, all of them test flights from Starbase, which is near the Texas border city of Brownsville. On the most recent jaunt, which lifted off on Sept. 28, Starship reached orbit for the first time and deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites — the first members of a new broadband constellation that could eventually consist of 100,000 spacecraft . Assembling that network will require a lot of Starship launches. And even more will be needed to build SpaceX's planned Starmind AI megaconstellation, which Elon Musk has said will harbor a million satellites . Indeed, the world's richest man has said that SpaceX is targeting more than 10,000 Starship liftoffs per year by 2030. Not all of those flights will originate from Starbase, which hosts two orbital pads. SpaceX is working to get three Starship pads up and running on Florida's Space Coast , and the company aims to break ground on a $100 billion, 12-pad complex in Louisiana next year. Each operational Starship launch will also feature two landings. Both of the vehicle's elements — the Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage — are designed to return to the pad after liftoff, where they will be caught by the tower's "chopstick" arms . So SpaceX's proposal for 456 launches from Starbase per year includes a request for approval for 912 landings. SpaceX plans to work up to this cadence in two phases, according to the FAA. Phase 1 "would include up to 100 annual launches and up to 200 annual landings (100 of Starship and 100 of Super Heavy)," the agency wrote. "Launches and landings could occur any day or time of the week." Phase 2 covers 456 launches and 912 landings, which would occur only Monday through Friday, though at any time on those days. The FAA will hold five "public scoping meetings" about the proposal next month, four of them in person in the Starbase area and one of them virtual. There will be two in-person meetings on Nov. 17 at Texas Southmost College, one from 1-3 p.m. local (Central) time and the other from 5:30-7:30 p.m. Two in-person meetings will follow on Nov. 19, at the same two times but at a different location: the Port Isabel Event & Cultural Center. The virtual meeting will be held N

item.title: Japanese consortium bets on building bobbing bit barns
item.description: A Japanese consortium wants to ease the datacenter space crunch by putting servers afloat – but keeping them moored safely alongside port quays. The group comprises shipping and logistics corporation NYK Line, engineering biz NTT Facilities, renewable energy developer Eurus Energy, and MUFG Bank. The quartet has also considered facilities farther out at sea, where they could draw on renewable energy sources such as offshore wind. Others are exploring wave power, including Oregon-based Panthalassa. However, the fab four acknowledge that offshore deployments still face practical hurdles, including maintenance access, high-capacity telecoms links, and independent power supplies. Keeping the floating facilities alongside a quay would let them use existing port infrastructure and nearby generation while the group works toward deployments well beyond the coast. Like others eyeing the waterfront, the consortium reckons bobbing bit barns could help meet growing compute demand without competing for scarce development land, though they would still need somewhere to plug in. We asked the consortium what capacity it expects the facilities to have, and when it anticipates these might be operational, but hadn't received a response at time of publication. NYK Line will oversee development, NTT Facilities will assess the designs, construction, and operation. Eurus Energy will explore renewable power supply, and MUFG Bank will consider financing related ventures. The consortium previously signed a memorandum of understanding with the city of Yokohama for a renewable-powered demonstration at the port. Testing began in March this year. The four may find they face competition in the floating compute farm stakes. Samsung Heavy Industries plans to dip a toe in, saying it expects to have its first facility operational by the second calendar quarter of 2028. ®

item.title: UK keeps AI safeguards in the maybe pile for Cyber Security BIll
item.description: UK officials have stopped short of committing to AI-specific measures in the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill despite ministers promising to legislate wherever necessary. The uncertainty comes amid warnings about autonomous AI threats, including Anthropic's forecast that small models could be months away from operating as self-replicating worms on vulnerable smart devices. Senior civil servants told MPs this week that the government was still considering amendments to the bill to address AI risks. Alexandra Jones, director general for growth, international, science and technology at the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade, is responsible for "AI and emerging technologies policy." However, she told MPs that the recent machinery-of-government changes had left the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport responsible for the Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill. "We are proposing… to use the Cyber Security Bill to consider changes to improve preparedness for AI, cyber, and loss of control risks… [to] look at how serious incidents and near misses are identified and reported, and how AI-driven disruption across the organizations is contained," she said. At Tuesday's Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee hearing, chair Liam Byrne interrupted: "You can't consider something in a bill. You have to legislate for something in a bill." AI minister Kanishka Narayan, who sits in the Cabinet Office, this week announced plans to "step up national defenses against growing AI risks." "We will use every power at our disposal. We will legislate wherever necessary. And we won't look to law alone. We will look to British ingenuity: our scientific expertise, technological capabilities and institutions to understand these increasingly powerful systems, defend against emerging threats and respond when things go wrong," he said. Asked about legislative changes, Jones said the government was "looking at" introducing amendments to the bill and "developing the policy to look at whether we use the Cyber Bill to do that." The UK has a decentralized, sector-specific approach to AI regulation. For example, the Information Commissioner's Office has published principles it will use to apply data protection law to AI. The EU's AI Act entered into force in August 2024, with new powers activated in stages. The US has no federal legislation specifically aimed at AI, although some states are introducing new laws. Anthropic's research, published on Monday, explored whether AI models could copy themselves between devices and run on the compromised hardware. item.content:encoded: UK officials have stopped short of committing to AI-specific measures in the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill despite ministers promising to legislate wherever necessary. The uncertainty comes amid warnings about autonomous AI threats, including Anthropic's forecast that small models could be months away from operating as self-replicating worms on vulnerable smart devices. Senior civil servants told MPs this week that the government was still considering amendments to the bill to address AI risks. Alexandra Jones, director general for growth, international, science and technology at the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade, is responsible for "AI and emerging technologies policy." However, she told MPs that the recent machinery-of-government changes had left the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport responsible for the Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill. "We are proposing… to use the Cyber Security Bill to consider changes to improve preparedness for AI, cyber, and loss of control risks… [to] look at how serious incidents and near misses are identified and reported, and how AI-driven disruption across the organizations is contained," she said. At Tuesday's Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee hearing, chair Liam Byrne interrupted: "You can't consider something in a bill. You have to legislate for something in a bill." AI minister Kanishka Narayan, who sits in the Cabinet Office, this week announced plans to "step up national defenses against growing AI risks." "We will use every power at our disposal. We will legislate wherever necessary. And we won't look to law alone. We will look to British ingenuity: our scientific expertise, technological capabilities and institutions to understand these increasingly powerful systems, defend against emerging threats and respond when things go wrong," he said. Asked about legislative changes, Jones said the government was "looking at" introducing amendments to the bill and "developing the policy to look at whether we use the Cyber Bill to do that." The UK has a decentralized, sector-specific approach to AI regulation. For example, the Information Commissioner's Office has published principles it will use to apply data protection law to AI. The EU's AI Act entered into force in August 2024, with new powers activated in stages. The US has no federal legislation specifically aimed at AI, although some states are introducing new laws. Anthropic's research, published on Monday, explored whether AI models could copy themselves between devices and run on the compromised hardware. Its forecast extrapolates from improving model capabilities, rather than demonstrating a fully autonomous worm spreading across real IoT devices. Consultancy Booz Allen Hamilton also warned that autonomous AI systems are fully capable of finding and attacking critical operational technology and industrial equipment, and shutting down access to water, power, and other daily life necessities. Earlier, AI risk researchers told the committee that model developers could not be trusted to regulate themselves, while international rules would have to overcome entrenched political differences. Daniel Kokotajlo, executive director of the AI Futures Project, said his nonprofit research organization had proposed a "least bad plan." "Don't do recursive self-improvement. Have a lot more transparency into the industry and a lot more regulation into the industry, so that it proceeds with the appropriate levels of transparency and caution. We think it's the least bad plan currently on the market. But it still has problems, and it would still be pretty scary to do," he said. Byrne summed up the testimony: "You have told us that the safety culture across the industry is catastrophic, that the safety culture in individual companies is in the wrong place, that the competitive dynamics between the companies are exacerbating these risks, that we cannot trust these companies to self-regulate." ®

item.title: From Mario to machine guns: how Ubisoft Paris made Tom Clancy’s Rainbow Six Tactics
item.description: The studio is swapping the Mushroom Kingdom’s vivid palette for the blood-soaked grit of military action series Where do you go after Mario? It’s a question the team at Ubisoft Paris found itself pondering three years ago after wrapping up work on the charming turn-based tactics adventure, Mario + Rabbids: Sparks of Hope , sequel to its unexpected crossover hit, Mario + Rabbids: Kingdom Battle. By melding a rather specialist genre with video gaming’s biggest household name, the developer introduced chin-stroking strategic play to a whole new audience. “ Having the opportunity to work with the Mario franchise was a privilege, and it’s still something I’m very proud of,” says level designer director, Julien Vial. “I still remember seeing the first prototype and being blown away by all the possibilities . ” Now, Ubisoft Paris has returned with a new project, but this time the studio is swapping the Mushroom Kingdom’s vivid palette for the blood-soaked grit of military action series Rainbow Six. Where Mario and Rabbids saw squishy creatures bounce harmlessly across levels as Mario encased foes in honey, Rainbow Six Tactics, a turn-based tactical spin-off from Rainbow Six Siege , sees balaclava-clad insurgents take shrapnel rounds to the chest. A seamless tonal shift, then. Continue reading...

item.title: After struggles v Spain, the USWNT’s midfield puzzle won’t be easily solved
item.description: The lack of cohesion in the center of the park is evident for the US, with Emma Hayes continuing to try different combinations The discourse around the US women’s national team may have been a harsh one if not for a fourth-half surge against Spain. In the latest of their back-to-back bookings, where Emma Hayes’ team plays the same opponent twice, Spain looked far more confident and effective than the four-time champions. Both teams were missing a handful of crucial players; Naomi Girma and Sam Coffey headlining the US’s absentees, while Aitana Bonmatí, Mariona Caldentey and Clàudia Pina were among Spain’s. Continue reading...
